analysis.one_liner: Funds free lawyers for poor tenants facing eviction and creates a national eviction database.
analysis.headline: The bill never left the Senate Banking Committee and died when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025, without a single cosponsor or a hearing.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would authorize $125 million a year, for five years, in grants to states and cities so tenants earning less than 125% of the federal poverty level could get a lawyer in eviction court. It would also spend $100 million a year to build a national HUD database of evictions, tracking who is evicted, why, and how often landlords file, and require a Government Accountability Office study on whether legal representation changes case outcomes.
analysis.who_benefits: Low-income tenants facing eviction, who in most courts today face a landlord's lawyer or file alone. Studies cited in the bill's own GAO mandate ask whether representation reduces default judgments and wrongful evictions. Cities and states would also gain funds to hire dedicated eviction-defense attorneys.

how_it_helps.text: Authorizes $125 million a year for fiscal years 2024 through 2028 in grants to states and local governments to hire attorneys dedicated to representing eligible tenants (income below 125% of the federal poverty level) in eviction cases. [S3]
Grants would be sized by a locality's eviction rate and how many tenants went unrepresented the prior year, with minimum grants of $1 million. [S3]

Requires HUD to build a national database of court-ordered, administrative, and illegal evictions, including tenant demographics, reasons for filing, whether tenants had lawyers, and repeat filings by the same landlords. [S3]
Requires a Government Accountability Office study on how the legal system fails tenants in eviction, the effect of full representation on outcomes, and potential cost savings. [S3]

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers, about $225 million a year if fully appropriated. Landlords would bear new reporting duties: courts and landlords would have to file detailed data on every eviction, and represented tenants are harder to remove.

drawbacks.text: The combined authorization is $225 million a year for five years, subject to appropriations, a real cost in a bill with no identified offset. [S3]

The database section imposes heavy reporting duties on state courts, clerks, law enforcement, and landlords, including detailed per-case and per-landlord data; compliance costs fall on state systems that vary widely. [S3]
Representation grants reach only tenants below 125% of the poverty line, so many working renters facing eviction would not qualify. [S3]
The bill does not create an automatic federal right to counsel; it relies on states to apply, and to show progress toward enacting their own right-to-counsel laws to qualify. [S3]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The direct benefit — a lawyer for a tenant facing loss of housing — is large for the individual, and eviction defense is cheap relative to the downstream costs of homelessness. The database is a genuine data-gathering good but its per-case reporting demands are ambitious and untested against state court capacity. The $225 million annual authorization is modest by federal standards but was never matched by appropriations politics or any cosponsor.

outcome.mechanism: Casey introduced the bill in December 2023 and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Banking Committee, which never took it up; with zero cosponsors and no further action, it expired when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Senator Robert Casey introduced the Eviction Prevention Act of 2023 on December 11, 2023. [S1]
The bill was read twice and referred the same day to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs, the only action it ever received. [S5]
No senator ever cosponsored the bill. [S4]
The committee took no further action, and the bill died at the end of the 118th Congress in January 2025 without a hearing, a markup, or a vote. [S5]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Landlords and rental owners avoid a federal eviction database and tenants with court-appointed counsel, and taxpayers avoid the cost; low-income tenants gained nothing.

for.name: Sen. Robert Casey Jr.
for.role: U.S. Senator from Pennsylvania, sole sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to committee; made no other recorded effort, and recruited no cosponsors.

against.name: Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Sen. Sherrod Brown (D-OH)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on December 11, 2023 and took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no floor consideration.

against.name: Sen. Sherrod Brown
against.role: Chair, Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee
against.what_they_did: As chair, controlled the committee calendar and never scheduled the bill for consideration before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a single Democratic sponsor and zero cosponsors of any party, so no partisan split ever formed; it died from inaction rather than a recorded vote.

industries.note: The bill would fund lawyers for tenants and log every eviction filing, landlord entity, rent, and fee into a national database. Represented tenants contest cases more effectively, and repeat-filing landlords would become visible to regulators and researchers.

industries.industry: Legal aid and eviction-defense legal services
industries.note: The bill directs $125 million a year to states and cities specifically to hire dedicated eviction-defense attorneys, a direct funding stream for the legal-services field.

industries.industry: Tenant screening and eviction data brokers
industries.note: A public national database could displace or complement commercial eviction-records products; the bill's privacy safeguards for tenants could cut both ways for firms that sell eviction history.
